Kanji Apps in 2026: How to Compare Current Options

Kanjidon Team · Feb 3, 2026

A dated feature table can look objective while mixing vendor claims, regional prices and untested judgments. This guide does not award one “best kanji app.” It shows how to verify current options from official sources and compare them with the same learning task. Disclosure: Kanjidon is our product, so any mention of it is not an independent recommendation.

Start with the Skill, Not the Brand

GoalEvidence the app should produceA representative test
Recognize kanjiClear contrast between similar formsDistinguish unfamiliar look-alikes in mixed order
Read vocabularyReadings taught in complete words and contextRead a studied word in a fresh sentence
Review over timeUnderstandable scheduling and honest failure handlingFail an item and inspect the normal return path
HandwriteA reference and input method suitable for your deviceWrite a word, then compare the form
Prepare for JLPTLanguage, reading and listening practice tied to official formatsCompare claims with official sample questions

Options to Verify on Their Official Pages

OptionQuestion to investigateOfficial source
KanjidonDoes the current app match the kanji, quiz and device workflow you want?Kanjidon website and current storefront listing
WaniKaniDoes its guided curriculum and review model fit your preferred level of control?WaniKani knowledge base
AnkiAre you willing to choose, verify and maintain the card content yourself?Official Anki site
Kanji StudyDoes the current Android listing provide the reference or writing workflow you need?Official Google Play listing
DuolingoDoes a broad Japanese course fit better than a kanji-focused workflow?Official Japanese character-practice guide

The questions are intentionally neutral. Product availability, feature scope and platform support can change, so follow each official source instead of treating this snapshot as a permanent specification.

Run the Same Trial Task

  • Choose the same small set of unfamiliar words.
  • Use each candidate’s normal onboarding and review path.
  • Test the words outside the app in a fresh sentence.
  • Record unclear prompts, setup work, accessibility barriers and duplicate reviews.
  • Keep only the tool whose evidence matches the job you defined.

Check Current Access and Subscription Terms

  • Read the current storefront and in-app purchase information for your region.
  • Identify which content remains available without payment.
  • Check renewal, cancellation and post-cancellation access.
  • Verify supported devices, account requirements and data synchronization.
  • Do not copy a price or free-tier description from an old review.

Inspect Privacy, Portability and Accessibility

Before building a large study history, check what data is collected, whether deletion or export is available and how the app behaves when you change devices. Test text size, color contrast, audio controls and input methods yourself; a marketing feature list cannot establish accessibility for your needs.

Avoid Multiple Competing Review Queues

A dictionary, reader and review tool can complement one another because they serve different tasks. Several schedulers covering the same vocabulary often create duplicate work. Choose one primary queue and add another tool only for a defined gap.

Make a Defensible Choice

  • The learning task matches your real goal.
  • The app tests knowledge outside a familiar card layout.
  • The workload remains understandable and sustainable.
  • Current access and payment terms are acceptable in your region.
  • Official documentation supports the features you are relying on.
  • The choice still leaves time for Japanese reading and listening.

  • Kanji Study official Google Play listing
